summary: This document specifies integrity and replay protection for the MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) and OLSRv2. It uses an HMAC-SHA-256 Integrity Check Value TLV and a Timestamp TLV.

plainLanguage.summary: In a wireless mesh network, the routers talk to each other directly, and any device in range can send them messages. This RFC makes those messages carry a seal that only a router holding the network's shared secret can produce, so a device that has not joined the network cannot inject routes of its own. It also puts a time stamp in each message, so that a message recorded earlier cannot be replayed later than the network's own tolerance for old messages.

questions: what is an integrity check value tlv
how does olsrv2 prevent replay attacks
subtitle: A required tamper seal and freshness stamp for the control messages of wireless mesh routing protocols.

tldr.problem: NHDP and OLSRv2 are the two routing protocols used in wireless mesh networks, and both accept control messages from anyone who can reach the network. Without a way to check that a message really came from a member of the network, and that it is not an old message replayed later, an attacker can inject routes or neighbour advertisements of their own.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires every message to carry an integrity check value, computed with HMAC-SHA-256 over the message and a shared secret key, and a timestamp TLV. A message whose integrity check value is missing or does not verify, or whose timestamp is too old, is rejected as badly formed.
tldr.outcome: Routers that hold the shared key ignore messages that do not carry a valid check value, so an attacker without the key cannot inject messages. Replay is limited to the age window that the timestamp allows, which depends on the clocks in the network being roughly in step.

today: RFC 7183 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes it. It updates RFC 6130 and RFC 7181, the two routing protocols it protects, and it depends on the ICV and TIMESTAMP TLV definitions of RFC 7182.

sections.title: What the Document Adds
sections.content:
This specification updates RFC 6130 and RFC 7181 by defining security mechanisms that implementations must include, for integrity and replay protection. A deployment of these protocols may choose to employ an alternative to these mechanisms: it may choose to protect packets rather than messages, it may choose to use an alternative integrity check value with preferred properties, and it may use an alternative timestamp. A deployment may choose to use no security mechanism at all, but this is not recommended.

The mechanisms specified are the use of an integrity check value (ICV) to protect the control messages of the protocols, and the use of timestamps in those messages to prevent replay attacks. Both use the TLV mechanism of RFC 5444 to carry this information in the message, and the ICV and TIMESTAMP TLVs themselves are defined in RFC 7182.

Different ICV TLVs are used for HELLO messages in NHDP and for TC (Topology Control) messages in OLSRv2. The HELLO ICV also protects the source address of the IP datagram that carries the message, because NHDP uses that address to determine the address of a neighbour interface and it is not necessarily otherwise contained in the HELLO message. An OLSRv2 TC message, by contrast, is forwarded in a new packet and so has no single IP datagram source address.
sections.plainLanguage:
NHDP is the protocol routers use to find out who their neighbours are, and OLSRv2 is the protocol that works out the routes. Both send control messages that any device nearby can send. This RFC says that each of those messages must carry a value that only a router with the shared key can compute, and a time stamp.

The two protocols need slightly different treatment. A HELLO message is used to work out which interface a neighbour is on, and the IP address the packet came from carries that information, so the check value covers that address too. A topology message is forwarded in a new packet each time, so it has no such address of its own.

sections.title: What the Mechanism Covers and What It Leaves Out
sections.content:
RFC 6130 and RFC 7181 allow specifications of extensions to recognise additional reasons for rejecting a message as badly formed and therefore invalid for processing, and they mention security, meaning integrity protection, as an explicit example. This document specifies such a mechanism.

Implementations of RFC 6130 and RFC 7181 MUST include this mechanism, and deployments SHOULD use it, except when a different security mechanism is more appropriate.

The applicability of the mechanism rests on five characteristics. It specifies a security mechanism that conforming implementations must include. It specifies an association of integrity check values with protocol messages, and how to use a missing or invalid value as a reason to reject a message as badly formed. It specifies an ICV Message TLV of RFC 7182 using a SHA-256-based Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) applied to the appropriate message contents, and for HELLO messages also to the IP datagram source address; implementations MUST support an HMAC-SHA-256 ICV TLV, and deployments SHOULD use it, and a message MAY carry more than one ICV TLV as long as each uses a different algorithm or key. It specifies the TIMESTAMP Message TLV of RFC 7182 for replay protection, using POSIX time where the clocks can be synchronised with sufficient precision. And it assumes that a router able to generate correct integrity check values is trusted.

Four things are deliberately left out. The document does not specify which key identifiers to use in a MANET where routers share more than one secret key; such keys are told apart by the key-id field of an ICV TLV. It does not specify how to distribute the cryptographic material. And it does not specify how to detect compromised routers that hold valid keys, nor how to revoke them.
sections.plainLanguage: The scope of the document is deliberately narrow. It says how to seal a message and how to check the seal, and it requires every implementation to support that. It does not say how the routers get the shared key in the first place, how to decide which of several keys to use, or what to do when a router that has the key turns out to be dishonest. Those are left to the deployment.

sections.title: Where the Check Sits
sections.content:
The mechanism is placed in the packet and message processing flow shown in Figure 1 of the RFC. It exists between the packet parsing and generation function of RFC 5444 and the message processing and generation function of NHDP and OLSRv2.

In the outgoing direction the mechanism specifies how to calculate an integrity check value for the message and how to include that value in an ICV Message TLV. In the incoming direction it verifies the ICV and TIMESTAMP TLVs contained in a message, so that a message can be rejected as badly formed and therefore invalid for processing before NHDP or OLSRv2 processes it. A message MUST be rejected if the ICV Message TLV is absent or its value cannot be verified.

That last rule has a consequence worth stating plainly: routers whose implementation does not include this specification will be ignored by routers that use it, and the two sets of routers will by design form disjoint MANETs. The unsecured MANET will retain some information about the secured one, but will be unable to use it, having no recognised symmetric links with it.

ICV Packet TLVs, also defined in RFC 7182, MAY be used by a deployment of the multiplexing process of RFC 5444, either as well as or instead of the protection of the NHDP and OLSRv2 messages. In the case of NHDP, packet protection is equally good and also protects the packet header. In the case of OLSRv2, packet protection has different properties from message protection, especially for some forms of ICV, and when a packet contains more than one message, packet protection has lower overheads in space and computation time.
sections.plainLanguage:
The check sits in the middle of the message handling, after the packet has been taken apart and before the routing protocol acts on what it found. On the way out it stamps the message; on the way in it checks the stamp and drops the message if the stamp does not match.

One consequence follows from the rule that a missing stamp means rejection: a router running an older implementation without this feature will not be recognised by the secured routers at all. The two groups end up as separate networks that cannot pass traffic between them.

sections.title: The Two Age Parameters
sections.content:
Two router parameters are specified for use by the two protocols. The first is required only by NHDP but may be visible to OLSRv2, and the second is required only by OLSRv2.

MAX_HELLO_TIMESTAMP_DIFF is the maximum age that a HELLO message to be validated may have. If the current POSIX time of the router validating the HELLO message, minus the timestamp in its TIMESTAMP TLV, is greater than this value, the HELLO message MUST be silently discarded. MAX_TC_TIMESTAMP_DIFF is the same thing for a TC message.

Both values must be greater than zero, but those bounds are not sufficient. Each MUST be at least as great as the maximum expected age of a message, that is the time between a message being sent by a router and reaching all its intended destinations. For a HELLO message this needs to cover a single hop, but a TC message may have been forwarded a number of times. For TC messages, if the jitter of RFC 7181 and RFC 5148 is used, the largest contribution to the age may be a delay of up to F_MAXJITTER per hop, except for the final hop. Other per-hop delays include the link layer used in the MANET and the CPU and memory resources of the routers, through queuing delays and delays for processing integrity check values. An implementation MAY set lower and upper bounds on these parameters, and MAY make its value of MAX_TC_TIMESTAMP_DIFF depend on the number of hops the message has travelled.

The constraints assume ideal time synchronisation of the clocks in all the routers. The parameters MAY be increased to allow for expected timing differences between routers, between neighbouring routers for MAX_HELLO_TIMESTAMP_DIFF and, allowing for greater separation, for MAX_TC_TIMESTAMP_DIFF. Excessively large values defeat the purpose of the parameters, so they SHOULD be as large as required and not significantly larger.

Using POSIX time allows a resolution of no more than one second, and in many MANET use cases time synchronisation much below one second is not possible because of unreliable and high-delay channels, mobility, interrupted communication and possible resource limitations. With the default message intervals and validity times of RFC 6130 and RFC 7181, where the shortest periodic message interval is 2 seconds, repeating a message within a second is actually beneficial rather than harmful, at a small bandwidth cost, and the use of jitter can make a message take that long or longer to cross the MANET, so even in a perfectly synchronised network the TC maximum delay would usually be greater than one second. A finer granularity than one second, and thus the use of an alternative timestamp, is however RECOMMENDED in cases where, possibly due to fast moving routers, message validity times are below one second.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each router has two settings: how old a HELLO message may be before it is thrown away, and the same for a topology message. Both must be larger than the time a message takes to reach its last recipient, or legitimate messages will be dropped. For a HELLO that is one hop, but a topology message may cross the whole network, and each hop adds a delay, so the setting for topology messages has to be much more generous.

Because the time stamp uses POSIX time, the resolution is one second. In a wireless network, where the channels are slow and the routers move, clocks that agree more closely than that are often not possible. Setting the limit too wide weakens the replay protection, so the value should be as small as the network can manage.

sections.title: What a Protected Message Must Contain
sections.content:
Messages must have the content specified in RFC 6130 and RFC 7181 respectively. In addition, a message that conforms to this mechanism must contain at least one ICV Message TLV, as specified in RFC 7182, and at least one TIMESTAMP Message TLV of the same specification.

Implementations must support a particular version of the ICV TLV, though other versions may be used instead or in addition in a deployment if more appropriate. For TC messages the type extension is 1, and for HELLO messages it is 2. The hash function is 3, which is SHA-256, and the cryptographic function is 3, which is HMAC. The ICV value MAY be truncated as specified in RFC 7182, and the selection of an appropriate length MAY be administratively configured. A message may contain several ICV Message TLVs.

For the TIMESTAMP TLV, implementations must support type extension 1, which is POSIX time, though other versions may be used instead or in addition.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protected message carries at least one seal and at least one time stamp. The seal is computed with HMAC and SHA-256, the standard combination for a keyed hash. The two message types use different numbers for the same seal format, so that a HELLO seal and a topology seal cannot be confused, and the seal may be shortened to save space.

sections.title: Adding the Seal to an Outgoing Message
sections.content:
After message generation, and before message transmission, the additional TLVs must be added to an outgoing message when using this mechanism. Six steps are defined for the case of a single timestamp version and a single ICV algorithm.

First, all ICV TLVs, if any, are temporarily removed from the message and stored, so that they can be reinserted later, and the message size and the Message TLV Block size are updated accordingly. Second, the msg-hop-count and msg-hop-limit fields, if present, are temporarily set to zero. Third, a TLV of type TIMESTAMP is added to the Message TLV Block, and the sizes are updated. Fourth, a TLV of type ICV is added, and the sizes are updated again. Fifth, the ICV TLVs removed in the first step are restored. Sixth, the hop count and hop limit fields are restored to their previous values.

An implementation MAY add alternative or additional TIMESTAMP and ICV TLVs. All TIMESTAMP TLVs MUST be inserted before adding the ICV TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: The order of operations matters. The old seal, if there is one, is taken out first, and the hop count and hop limit are set to zero, so that the value covers the message in a form that is the same on every hop. The time stamp goes in next, then the seal is computed over the message with the time stamp in place. The old seal is then put back, and the hop count and limit are restored, because they change as the message is forwarded.

sections.title: Checking an Incoming Message
sections.content:
Both RFC 6130 and RFC 7181 require a router to first check whether an incoming message is invalid for processing, and they list a number of conditions that each lead to a rejection of the message as badly formed and therefore invalid for processing. When using a single timestamp version and a single ICV algorithm, four further conditions are added to that list, each of which must cause NHDP or OLSRv2 to consider the message invalid.

The first is that the Message TLV Block does not contain exactly one TIMESTAMP TLV of the selected version, where the version specification includes the type extension. The block may also contain TIMESTAMP TLVs of other versions. The second is that the block does not contain exactly one ICV TLV using the selected algorithm and key identifier, where the algorithm specification includes the type extension and, for type extensions 1 and 2, the hash function and the cryptographic function. The block may also contain ICV TLVs using other algorithms and key identifiers.

The third condition is that validation of the identified TIMESTAMP TLV fails. For a TIMESTAMP TLV with type extension 1, validation fails if the current POSIX time minus the value in that TLV is greater than MAX_HELLO_TIMESTAMP_DIFF for a HELLO message or MAX_TC_TIMESTAMP_DIFF for a TC message; otherwise it succeeds. If a deployment chooses a type extension other than 1, appropriate measures must be taken to verify the freshness of the message.

The fourth condition is that validation of the identified ICV TLV fails. To validate it, all ICV Message TLVs are temporarily removed from the message and the sizes updated, the hop count and hop limit fields are temporarily set to zero, and the ICV is calculated for the parameters in the identified TLV. If this ICV differs from the value in the TLV, validation fails; if the value has been truncated, the calculated value must be truncated to the same length before the comparison. Otherwise validation succeeds, the hop count and limit are restored, and the ICV TLVs are returned to the message.
sections.plainLanguage:
A received message has to pass four tests: there is exactly one time stamp of the agreed version, there is exactly one seal of the agreed algorithm, the time stamp is recent enough, and the seal matches the message.

The last test is done by taking the seal out of the message, zeroing the hop count and limit so that the calculation is the same as it was at the sender, recomputing the seal, and comparing it with the one that arrived. A mismatch means the message was altered in flight, or came from someone without the key.

sections.title: What It Stops and What It Does Not
sections.content:
The document specifies a security mechanism for NHDP and OLSRv2 that mitigates several threats.

Identity spoofing, where an attacker falsely claims the identity of a valid router, is countered, because only routers possessing the selected shared secret key are able to add a valid ICV TLV to a message. When one shared key is used for all the routers in the MANET, however, it is only possible to tell that a router is valid, not to tell which router it is, so a malicious router holding the valid key may still spoof the identity of another router using the same key. Link spoofing, where an attacker falsely represents the existence of a nonexistent link or otherwise misrepresents the state of a link, is countered on the same argument.

Replay attacks are partly countered, but this depends on synchronised clocks in the MANET. An attacker that records messages to replay them later can only do so within the time interval allowed after the timestamp in the message, because the attacker cannot modify the timestamp, which is protected by the integrity check value. Within that interval replay is still possible, and the limits on the interval are set so that this has a limited effect on the operation of the protocol.

The limitations are stated plainly. If no synchronised clocks are available, replay attacks cannot be countered by this mechanism at all; an alternative version of the TIMESTAMP TLV with a monotonic sequence number may have some partial value, but needs state to record the observed sequence numbers. The mechanism does not avoid or detect attacks by routers that hold the shared secret key used to generate the integrity check values. It relies on an out-of-band mechanism for distributing the shared key and any additional cryptographic parameters, and it provides no key management mechanism; Section 23.6 of RFC 7181 discusses at length why the automated key management requirements of RFC 4107 do not apply to OLSRv2 and NHDP.
sections.plainLanguage:
The mechanism stops an outside device from injecting messages, because it cannot compute the seal. It also limits replay: a recorded message can only be sent again within the window that the time stamp allows, because the time stamp itself is covered by the seal and cannot be changed.

Two limits are worth knowing. The replay protection depends on the clocks in the network being roughly in step, and where they are not, replay cannot be stopped at all. And the mechanism does nothing about a router that has the key and is dishonest, because such a router can produce a perfectly valid seal.
